item.title: A “Natural Ozempic” Discovered by AI?
item.description:
Appetite

A “Natural Ozempic” Discovered by AI?

Newly identified peptide may have fewer side effects than current GLP-1 drugs.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • AI helped identify BRP, a naturally occurring peptide that may reduce appetite.
  • BRP reduced food intake and body fat in animals without clear nausea or muscle loss.
  • BRP appears to act through brain pathways different from those targeted by GLP-1 drugs.
  • Despite promising animal results, BRP has not yet been tested for safety or efficacy in humans.
Source: Joachim Schnürle / Pixabay

The success of drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy has transformed how scientists think about obesity. These medications demonstrate that appetite and body weight are not simply products of willpower. They are regulated by biological signals connecting the brain, digestive system, pancreas, and other organs.

But the same broad biological reach that makes these drugs effective can also produce unwanted effects, including nausea, constipation, slowed digestion, and loss of lean body mass.

Now, researchers at Stanford Medicine have identified a naturally occurring molecule that may suppress appetite through a different, and potentially more targeted, pathway. The molecule, called BRP (short for BRINP2-related peptide), reduced food intake and body weight in mice and pigs without producing several of the adverse effects associated with existing weight-loss medications.

Headlines have understandably referred to BRP as a “natural Ozempic.” That comparison captures the excitement surrounding the discovery, but it also risks getting ahead of the science. BRP has not yet been shown to be safe or effective in humans.

What may be most important about the research is not that scientists have found an immediate replacement for semaglutide. It is that artificial intelligence (AI) helped uncover a previously hidden biological signal that may lead to an entirely new class of obesity treatments.

Searching the Body’s Hidden Pharmacy

Our bodies manufacture thousands of proteins, many of which begin as larger, inactive precursors called prohormones. Enzymes cut these prohormones into smaller fragments known as peptides. Some peptides become hormones that regulate appetite, metabolism, stress, growth, and other essential functions.

The problem is that biologically meaningful peptides are difficult to find. They can be buried among thousands of fragments produced during ordinary protein processing.

Instead of attempting to isolate every possible peptide in the laboratory, the Stanford team developed a computational tool called Peptide Predictor. The algorithm examined approximately 20,000 human protein-coding genes for locations where enzymes might cut prohormones into biologically active peptides.

The researchers focused on cleavage patterns associated with prohormone convertase 1/3, an enzyme involved in producing several hormones, including glucagon-like peptide-1, or GLP-1. Semaglutide works by mimicking GLP-1’s effects.

The algorithm narrowed the search to 373 possible prohormones and predicted that they could generate 2,683 peptides. Researchers selected 100 candidates that appeared likely to act in the brain and tested them in neuron-like cells.

One peptide stood out: BRP.

The molecule was only 12 amino acids long, yet it increased neuronal activity approximately tenfold, compared with untreated cells.

The discovery illustrates one of AI’s most promising roles in medicine. AI did not independently invent a weight-loss drug or prove that the molecule works. It helped researchers navigate a vast biological search space and identify candidates that might otherwise have remained overlooked.

What BRP Did in Animals

The researchers next administered BRP to mice and minipigs. Pigs were included because aspects of their metabolism and eating behavior resemble those of humans more closely than mouse models alone.

A BRP injection given before feeding reduced food consumption during the following hour by as much as 50 percent in both species. Obese mice receiving daily injections for 14 days lost an average of about three grams, almost entirely from body fat, while untreated mice gained approximately three grams. The treated mice also showed improved glucose and insulin tolerance.

Equally intriguing was what the researchers did not observe. The animals did not display clear signs of nausea, food aversion, constipation, reduced water consumption, abnormal movement, or anxiety-like behavior. The weight reduction also did not appear to involve substantial muscle loss.

These findings raise the possibility that BRP could influence appetite more selectively than current GLP-1 medications.

GLP-1 receptors are distributed throughout the brain, digestive tract, pancreas, and other tissues. That widespread distribution helps explain semaglutide’s effects on appetite, blood glucose, and digestion. BRP appears to activate different neuronal and metabolic pathways and may act more specifically within the hypothalamus, a brain region central to hunger and energy regulation.

A treatment that reduces appetite without broadly affecting the digestive system would represent an important advance. But that possibility remains hypothetical.

Source: Nancy Mure / Pixabay

Why “Natural” Does Not Mean Proven—or Safer

Describing BRP as natural may make it sound inherently gentle or safe. But natural molecules can have powerful biological effects, and a substance naturally produced by the body can behave differently when administered at pharmacological doses.

Researchers have not yet identified the receptor through which BRP acts. They also do not know whether humans will respond as mice and pigs did, whether repeated treatment could produce unforeseen effects, or whether appetite suppression would be sustained over time.

Another challenge is that small peptides are often broken down rapidly in the body. The researchers are exploring ways to extend BRP’s activity, but modifying the molecule to last longer could also change its effectiveness or safety profile.

A New Direction for Obesity Treatment

Obesity is a complex, chronic condition shaped by genetics, metabolism, medications, sleep, stress, environment, mental health, food access, and social conditions. No single molecule will address every cause or work for every person.

Still, BRP represents an encouraging shift. Rather than merely modifying existing GLP-1 drugs, scientists may be able to identify previously unknown hormones and brain pathways that regulate appetite with greater precision.

The discovery also challenges the persistent idea that hunger should be controllable through discipline alone. Appetite emerges from complex neural and hormonal systems, many of which operate outside conscious awareness.

BRP is not yet a natural alternative to Ozempic. It is an early-stage experimental molecule supported by promising animal data. Human trials will determine whether that promise survives the difficult transition from laboratory discovery to medical treatment.

For now, the real breakthrough may be the method: using AI to reveal biological messages the human body has been sending all along.

item.title: You Don't Need Sexual Attraction to Have Great Sex
item.description:
Low Sexual Desire

You Don't Need Sexual Attraction to Have Great Sex

What science, psychology, and long-term couples can teach us about desire.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • Sexual desire naturally fluctuates over the course of long-term relationships.
  • We tend to glorify the sexual spark because it is dramatic and easy to recognize.
  • Sexual attraction is only one pathway to arousal. There are many others.
  • Relationships are transformed based on biology and psychology.

I'm about to make a statement that may cause some of you to stop reading and shake your head.

Here it is: You don't need to be sexually attracted to your partner to have great sex.

As a psychotherapist, I've shared that idea with countless clients over the years. Almost every time, the reaction is the same. A puzzled look or nervous laughter.

I ask my clients to stay with me because I'm not suggesting that attraction doesn't matter. I'm suggesting something far more interesting.

Sexual attraction is only one pathway to arousal.

It is not the only one.

Meaningful touch is a gateway to arousal.

Authentic words spoken at the right time is a gateway to arousal.

Quiet, uninterrupted time can be a gateway to arousal.

Being admired by the person you love can be a gateway to arousal.

Understanding that we can access many gateways to arousal has transformed a number of marriages that were once headed toward Splitsville.

I call on the life advice my grandparents gifted me with frequently in my work these days. I learned the perfect metaphor for relationship transitions years ago in my Grandma Maybelle's kitchen.

When I was a kid, I would stand in her kitchen eating fresh strawberries by the handful. They were sweet and juicy. But then something interesting happened. Months later, when summer was long gone, those very same strawberries appeared on my morning toast as homemade preserves.

They weren't the same. Yet somehow they were just as satisfying, perhaps even better. The fresh berries had been transformed into something richer, deeper, and meant to be savored rather than devoured.

Long-term relationships can follow the same path.

In the beginning, love is fueled by excitement and the intoxicating rush of raw physical attraction. Everything feels effortless because everything is new. Over time, relationships evolve. Excitement matures into familiarity. Passion becomes intertwined with trust, emotional safety, shared history, inside jokes, resilience, and the quiet comfort of being deeply known.

Many people mistake this transformation for loss. I think we've been trained to feel this way.

Movies, social media, dating apps, and even well-meaning relationship advice often equate passion with perpetual excitement. They sell the fantasy that if the butterflies disappear, something must be wrong.

That is not true. Relationships are transformed based on biology and psychology.

Longitudinal research has consistently shown that sexual desire naturally fluctuates over the course of long-term relationships. Declining desire is common and does not necessarily signal that love has disappeared or that the relationship is failing. Yet, because few people are prepared for this normal transition, many couples panic when they arrive there. They assume the relationship has lost something essential when it may simply be changing form (especially if the couple’s friendship and warm connected feelings remain intact).

In my therapy practice, I've watched countless couples fall into despair because they interpreted a predictable season of their relationship as a permanent diagnosis. What they believed was the end of desire often turned out to be the beginning of a different kind of desire altogether.

Like Grandma Maybelle's strawberries, the ingredients were still there. They had simply changed recipes.

A client, whom I'll call Max, sat across from me during an initial therapy session. He had been married for eleven years. He said, "I love my wife. God knows I do. We never had sexual chemistry that was off the charts, but whatever we had feels completely gone."

He paused before adding, "The other night we went out on a date. She put so much effort into getting ready. She wore this beautiful dress and a pair of strappy heels. She looked great. It did... nothing for me. I hate even saying that out loud because I really do love her."

I nodded with genuine empathy. Then, I thought.. Have I got some good news for you, buddy!

Over the next several months, something remarkable happened. His anxiety gave way to curiosity. His discouragement gave way to hope. Eventually, he described their physical relationship as warm, sensual, deeply connected, and more satisfying than it had been in years.

So, what changed? It wasn’t his wife, her body, or the way she dressed.

From a psychological perspective, Max had unknowingly been preprogramming every intimate experience with the same message:

"There's nothing here."

His brain and his body obeyed him.

Every time he looked at his wife, he was evaluating whether she generated the same spark he expected eleven years earlier. When she didn't, his brain interpreted the experience as proof that the attraction was gone.

One day I asked him a different question. "What keeps you grounded in this marriage?"

Without hesitation, he answered, "I still love her. I deeply respect her. She's my best friend. We've built a beautiful life together. We've raised two incredible kids. She's been beside me through some of the hardest moments of my life."

"There it is. That’s your gateway to arousal. That’s not nothing. That is something. " I said.

What grounds you inside the relationships can also be the doorway used to access arousal that often leads to satisfying sex.

Yes, a pair of perfectly fitted jeans can be sexy. But so is a woman who stood beside you when your father died; the person who believed in you when your confidence disappeared; the friend you survived financial stress, health scares, and family conflict with.

That is a different kind of sexy — a grounded kind, built from emotional safety, admiration, trust, loyalty, gratitude, and shared history.

Psychologically speaking, arousal doesn't begin in the body. It begins in the meaning our minds assign to another person.

When Max stopped asking, "Am I wildly attracted to my wife?" and started asking, "Who is this remarkable woman I've shared my life with?" his attention and emotions shifted.

Then his body shifted.

During our last therapy session, Max commented, “It’s crazy that the familiarity I had thought was working against us brought us back together. It was my thinking!”

The irony is that many couples spend years mourning the loss of youthful chemistry while overlooking a richer source of desire that has been growing beneath the surface all along.

Sometimes a mindset shift is the spark to deep intimacy.

Perhaps it's time we stopped asking couples:

"Are you still sexually attracted to each other?"

And begin asking a better question:

"Which gateway to arousal are you walking through today?"

We tend to glorify the spark because it is dramatic and easy to recognize. Yet many of the strongest and most enduring intimate relationships are sustained by a different kind of energy: one that is less explosive, but far more stable.

The couples who continue to experience deeply satisfying sex over the long haul aren't necessarily the ones who never lost the butterflies. More often, they are the ones who learned that desire can be intentionally accessed through many doors.

They stopped waiting to feel attracted and began noticing everything there was to appreciate, admire, and cherish about the person beside them.

The mind responded. The body followed.

Perhaps the greatest gift long-term love offers isn't endless novelty. It's the opportunity to discover that the deepest forms of desire are often rooted in everything the two of you have become together.
